## Summary
- special-case GLM-style chat templates during `auto` content-format detection
- keep these templates on the `string` path when they require raw string tool responses
- add renderer regressions for format detection and prompt rendering of tool results

Fixes #39614.

## Why this is not duplicating an existing PR
- I checked open PRs that reference `#39614` and did not find another open PR for this issue.
- I also checked nearby GLM-related PRs; the open PR `#39253` is about GLM tool parser streaming and does not address prompt rendering of tool result content.

## Root cause
`resolve_chat_template_content_format(..., given_format="auto", ...)` classified certain GLM templates as `openai` because they iterate over `message.content` for regular messages. That causes tool-role messages to be converted into OpenAI-style structured content items before rendering. For GLM templates that explicitly expect `m.content is string` for tool responses, the rendered prompt then falls into the wrong branch and emits an empty `<tools>` wrapper instead of the actual tool result text.

## Tests run
- `python -m py_compile vllm/renderers/hf.py tests/renderers/test_hf.py` ✅
- `python -m pytest --noconftest tests/renderers/test_hf.py -k "glm_tool_response_template" -q` ❌
  - blocked by local environment mismatch during import: the machine's installed `torch` is older than current vLLM expects (`torch.library.infer_schema` is missing)

## AI assistance
This PR was prepared with AI assistance. I reviewed the changed files, commit, and PR description before submission.

## Code Review

This pull request introduces a heuristic to correctly identify GLM-family chat templates that require raw string tool responses, preventing tool outputs from being dropped when the template is incorrectly classified as OpenAI-style. It includes a new detection function `_looks_like_glm_tool_response_template` and corresponding unit tests. Feedback suggests that the current string-matching heuristic for detecting these templates is fragile and could be improved with regular expressions or AST analysis to handle variations in Jinja syntax, such as different spacing or bracket notation.

![high](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/high-priority.svg)

The heuristic used to detect GLM tool response templates is quite fragile as it relies on exact string matching for Jinja code. Specifically, the check for `role == 'tool'` (lines 292-293) will fail if the template uses different spacing (e.g., `role=='tool'`) or bracket notation (e.g., `message['role'] == 'tool'`), which is common in many chat templates. 

While this targeted fix addresses the specific GLM templates identified, a more robust approach would be to use a regular expression to handle whitespace variations and different quote types, or to perform a more detailed AST analysis to find the `role` comparison logic.

+{%- if m.role == 'user' -%}

+{%- if m.content is iterable and m.content is not string and m.content is not mapping -%}
+{%- for item in m.content -%}
+{%- if item is mapping and item.type == 'text' -%}{{ item.text }}{%- endif -%}

+{%- set tc = tc.function -%}
+{%- endif -%}
+<tool_call>{{ tc.name }}{% for k, v in tc.arguments.items() %}<arg_key>{{ k }}</arg_key><arg_value>{{ v }}</arg_value>{% endfor %}</tool_call>
+{%- endfor -%}
+{%- endif -%}
+{%- elif m.role == 'tool' -%}
+<|observation|>
+{%- if m.content is string -%}
+<tool_response>{{ m.content }}</tool_response>
+{%- else -%}
+<tool_response><tools>
+{%- for tr in m.content -%}
+{{ tr.name }}
+{%- endfor -%}
+</tools></tool_response>
+{%- endif -%}
+{%- endif -%}
+{%- endfor -%}"""
